title: Beyond the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: Colormap Assessment through Data-Aware Perceptual Metric
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, IEEE VIS 2026 conference full paper
summary: Continuous colormaps are widely used to visualize scalar fields, and their quality is typically evaluated using measures such as discriminative power and uniformity. Existing measures primarily characterize the intrinsic perceptual properties of the colormap itself, largely independent of the underlying data distribution. In practice, however, user perception arises not from the colormap alone but from the visualization generated by mapping data values through the colormap. The perceptual differences that users actually experience depend jointly on the colormap and the underlying data. We propose a data-aware formulation that complements existing data-independent colormap assessment approaches. Rather than analyzing the colormap in isolation, we model the color-encoded visualization as a composite mapping from the spatial domain of the data to perceptual color space. This approach yields data-aware counterparts of established measures, including discriminative power, uniformity, and smoothness, as well as additional measures such as perceptual anisotropy and degeneracy. We validate the proposed measures against both the existing data-independent framework and empirical results from perceptual studies, extend the formulation to 2D colormaps, and demonstrate its integration into colormap optimization. An interactive system is provided for exploring colormap assessment under varying data distributions. Results demonstrate that our formulation offers a principled foundation for data-aware colormap assessment and design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a data-aware framework for evaluating continuous colormaps by analyzing the perceptual properties of the final visualization, rather than the colormap alone. It derives data-dependent versions of established metrics, adds new measures, validates them empirically, extends them to 2D colormaps, and applies them to colormap optimization.
AI.motivation: Conventional colormap metrics assess intrinsic properties such as discriminative power and uniformity independently of the data being visualized. However, perceived differences are determined by the interaction between the colormap and the data distribution. The paper addresses this gap by developing an assessment framework that reflects perception of the actual color-encoded visualization.
AI.method: The authors model visualization as a composite mapping from the data's spatial domain through scalar or multidimensional data values into perceptual color space. Based on this formulation, they define data-aware counterparts of discriminative power, uniformity, and smoothness, and introduce perceptual anisotropy and degeneracy measures. The framework is evaluated against data-independent colormap measures and perceptual-study findings, generalized to 2D colormaps, integrated into colormap optimization, and implemented in an interactive exploration system.
AI.result: The proposed measures capture perceptual behavior that depends on the underlying data distribution and provide results consistent with empirical perceptual studies. The framework supports assessment of both 1D and 2D colormaps and can guide colormap optimization. The interactive system demonstrates practical exploration of how different data distributions affect colormap quality.
AI.conclusion: Colormap quality should be evaluated as a property of the combined data-to-color visualization mapping, not solely of the colormap. The proposed data-aware formulation provides a principled complement to existing data-independent methods and supports more effective colormap assessment and design.

title: EvoMaestro: Toward Interpretable and Steerable LLM-Driven Program Evolution
summary: Recent program evolution systems use large language models (LLMs) to generate and iteratively improve populations of programs, producing striking advances in mathematics, algorithm design, and scientific computing. Yet these systems largely operate as fully automated black boxes. As populations grow, domain experts must make sense of the scores, code changes, reasoning, and algorithmic ideas across many programs, while current interfaces provide limited support for understanding or redirecting the evolution. We characterize this need to understand and steer populations of evolving algorithmic ideas as semantic oversight. A formative study with 8 domain experts yields six design requirements for this emerging human-computer interaction problem. We then propose a steerable program evolution framework that lets expert judgments shape subsequent evolution. Built on this framework, EvoMaestro is an interactive visual analytics system that organizes evolution information from population overview to source code. It helps experts locate and compare noteworthy programs, guide evolution with natural language, combine promising ideas, and prune unproductive directions. A seven-day system demonstration illustrates how an expert applied these capabilities throughout a long-running evolution process. A within-subjects study with 12 participants shows that EvoMaestro improves users' understanding of evolution processes, reduces cognitive workload, and supports expert steering. These findings suggest that preserving expert agency in open-ended LLM-driven search requires support for both informed judgment and the ability to shape subsequent automation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EvoMaestro, an interactive visual analytics system for understanding and steering LLM-driven program evolution. It combines population-level exploration, code comparison, natural-language guidance, idea recombination, and pruning. Studies with domain experts and general participants indicate improved understanding, lower cognitive workload, and effective expert control.
AI.motivation: LLM-based program evolution can generate strong algorithms, but existing systems are largely opaque and autonomous. As populations expand, domain experts struggle to interpret scores, code changes, reasoning, and emerging ideas, and they have limited ability to redirect the search. The paper frames this challenge as semantic oversight and investigates how interfaces can preserve expert agency during open-ended automated evolution.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a formative study with 8 domain experts to derive six design requirements. They then develop a steerable program evolution framework and implement EvoMaestro, an interactive visual analytics system that connects population overviews with source-code details. The system supports finding and comparing notable programs, issuing natural-language steering instructions, merging promising ideas, and pruning unproductive search directions. Evaluation includes a seven-day system demonstration with one expert and a within-subjects study involving 12 participants.
AI.result: The formative study identifies six requirements for semantic oversight. The demonstration shows that an expert can use EvoMaestro throughout a long-running evolution process to inspect results and redirect subsequent search. The within-subjects study reports improved understanding of evolution processes, reduced cognitive workload, and support for expert steering when using the system.
AI.conclusion: Effective oversight of LLM-driven program evolution requires more than displaying generated artifacts. Systems should support both informed interpretation of evolving populations and direct expert intervention in subsequent automation. EvoMaestro demonstrates one approach to maintaining expert agency through integrated visual analytics and steering mechanisms.

title: Judgement and the Feeling of Agency When Instructing a Computer to Act
summary: In cognitive psychology, the sense of agency refers to the feeling of controlling an external event through one's own actions. This paper asks how people experience agency when they give an instruction to a computer, which then acts on their behalf. Research in human-human interaction has found that while people experience agency over the initial actions taken by another in response to their command, they may not experience agency over the ultimate outcome of those actions. We present two experiments. The first draws on prior studies of human-to-human interaction but replaces a human co-actor with a computer. The second study addresses potential limitations in the first, exploring the effect of more meaningful outcomes, and assessing both pre-reflective feelings and post-reflective judgements of agency. We find that participants experienced agency over the initial action taken by the computer in response to their command, but did not experience pre-reflective agency over the final outcome. Interestingly, however, they did judge themselves to have caused the final outcome when it was meaningful and their command specific. This difference between the pre-reflective feeling and post-reflective judgement of agency has important implications for design. If designers want people to feel in control and take responsibility for outcomes that result from instructions given to a computer, they cannot rely on pre-reflective intuition. Instead, we should design systems that encourage people to reflect on their actions and make deliberative judgments regarding responsibility.

AI.tldr: The paper examines whether people feel and judge themselves to be agents of outcomes produced by a computer acting on their instructions. Across two experiments, participants felt agency over the computer’s immediate action but not over the final outcome at a pre-reflective level; meaningful outcomes and specific commands increased reflective judgments of responsibility. The findings distinguish intuitive agency from deliberative responsibility and suggest design strategies that promote reflection.
AI.motivation: The study is motivated by the growing role of computer systems that execute instructions and produce outcomes on users’ behalf. Prior human-human research suggests that agency may extend to an intermediary’s initial response but weaken for the ultimate result. The paper investigates whether this pattern also applies to human-computer interaction and whether meaningful outcomes and reflective evaluation alter perceived agency.
AI.method: Two experiments were conducted. Experiment 1 adapted human-human interaction paradigms by replacing the human co-actor with a computer. Experiment 2 addressed limitations of the first experiment by using more meaningful outcomes and separately measuring pre-reflective feelings of agency and post-reflective judgments of agency. The studies also manipulated or assessed command specificity.
AI.result: Participants reported or exhibited agency over the computer’s initial action following their instruction, but lacked pre-reflective agency over the final outcome. When the outcome was meaningful and the command was specific, participants nevertheless judged themselves to have caused the final outcome. Thus, intuitive feelings of agency and reflective judgments of causal responsibility diverged.
AI.conclusion: Agency in human-computer interaction is layered: immediate action control may generate a sense of agency, whereas downstream outcomes may not produce an intuitive feeling of control. However, reflection can lead users to attribute responsibility to themselves, particularly for meaningful outcomes following specific instructions. Systems intended to support user control and accountability should encourage deliberate reflection rather than rely solely on users’ spontaneous feelings of agency.

title: No speech articulator robustly favours retroauricular electrodes over canonical jaw sites: a volume-conductor model with orientation and electrode-count controls
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures. Code, electrode definitions and result tables: https://github.com/Somach-Systems-Inc/ear-emg-forward-model
summary:
Objective. Ear-worn biopotential devices are being designed around a coupling that has not been computed: how strongly each speech articulator reaches electrodes on the jaw and around the ear. We compute it, and test the answer against the three things that could produce it spuriously - source orientation, electrode count, and the level of anatomical detail in the volume conductor.
  Approach. Articulator-to-electrode coupling is computed by reciprocity on MIDA, a head model with 116 labelled compartments at 500 microns, treating muscle as both the generator and its own conducting compartment. Twenty-two electrode positions - spanning the canonical jaw montage, a retroauricular cluster, and a cEEGrid C-path - are compared against ten individually segmented articulators. Source orientation is swept over the hemisphere, not assumed, and every comparison is repeated at matched electrode counts.
  Results. Five articulators - orbicularis oris, buccinator, mentalis, depressor anguli oris, and platysma - favour the jaw montage at every sampled orientation and at every electrode subsample. No muscle robustly favours the retroauricular montage. The strongest ear-leaning candidate, temporalis, reaches -2.57 dB under a uniform orientation sweep; but derived from the label volume, its fibre field gives -1.15 dB with an interval of [-1.45, +5.46], and only half of four-site retroauricular subsets favour the ear.
  Significance. For device design the result is one-sided, not a trade: a retroauricular montage loses lip and chin activity entirely and buys no muscle back reliably in exchange. What remains a design lever is placement - a four-site cluster chosen by anatomical target outperforms arbitrary placement around the ear by up to 1.07 dB.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies how strongly speech-articulator muscles couple to jaw-mounted versus ear-adjacent electrodes using reciprocity in a detailed head model. It finds that five perioral and lower-face muscles consistently favor the jaw montage, while no muscle robustly favors retroauricular electrodes. Electrode placement within the ear region remains an optimization variable, but the broader design conclusion favors jaw placement for comprehensive articulator coverage.
AI.motivation: Ear-worn biopotential systems are being developed without a quantitative account of which speech articulators are detectable at electrodes on or near the jaw and ear. The study addresses this gap and tests whether apparent montage advantages could instead be artifacts of source orientation, electrode number, or anatomical-model resolution.
AI.method: The authors compute articulator-to-electrode coupling through reciprocity using the high-resolution MIDA head model, which contains 116 anatomical compartments at 500-micron resolution. Ten individually segmented articulators are modeled as both signal-generating muscles and conducting tissues. Coupling is evaluated for 22 electrode locations spanning a canonical jaw montage, a retroauricular cluster, and a cEEGrid-like C-path. Source orientations are swept across a hemisphere rather than fixed, and comparisons are repeated with matched electrode counts to control for montage size.
AI.result: Orbicularis oris, buccinator, mentalis, depressor anguli oris, and platysma consistently favor the jaw montage across all tested orientations and electrode subsamples. No muscle robustly favors the retroauricular montage. Temporalis is the strongest possible ear-leaning candidate, reaching -2.57 dB under a uniform orientation sweep; however, its anatomically derived fibre field yields only -1.15 dB with a broad interval of [-1.45, +5.46] dB, and only half of the four-electrode retroauricular subsets favor the ear. Within the ear region, target-informed four-site placement can outperform arbitrary placement by up to 1.07 dB.
AI.conclusion: The evidence supports an asymmetric design conclusion rather than a trade-off: retroauricular electrodes lose reliable access to lip and chin activity without consistently recovering another articulator. Jaw montages therefore provide more dependable coverage of the studied speech muscles. If ear-worn hardware is required, electrode placement should be optimized for the intended anatomical target rather than chosen arbitrarily.

title: From Community Values to AI Design Constraints: A Mixed-Methods Study of a Proposed AI-Driven Wildfire Risk Assessment Tool in Los Angeles County
summary: AI-driven hazard tools are increasingly proposed for resident-facing risk communication. However, residents are often asked for feedback only after decisions about data use, privacy, and explanation have been made. This study takes an earlier approach by examining residents' values, concerns, and practical expectations for a proposed AI-based risk assessment tool before a predictive model or functional interface is developed. The proposed smartphone application would use property photographs to estimate parcel-level wildfire risk and provide an interpretable risk score, uncertainty information, and mitigation recommendations. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, we surveyed 30 Los Angeles County residents, seven of whom also participated in a virtual town hall. We analyzed the data using descriptive statistics, exploratory FDR-adjusted Spearman correlations, and inductive thematic coding of open-ended and town hall responses. Participants were cautiously receptive: 66.7% said they would be very likely or likely to use the tool. They linked fair risk assessment to whether the tool considered relevant property and neighborhood conditions. Privacy and data security were the most common concerns (64.3%), while cost was the main barrier to acting on recommendations (65.5%). Likelihood of using the tool was strongly associated with likelihood of saving or sharing risk results ($ρ= 0.752$, $p_{\mathrm{FDR}} < .001$). We translated the findings into the AI Value Map, a community-grounded artifact with nine value dimensions. The Map connects participant findings to provisional design requirements and possible consequences if they are not addressed. This study provides exploratory evidence on residents' responses to a proposed AI wildfire tool and offers a pre-model procedure for translating early community input into traceable design constraints for resident-facing AI hazard tools.

AI.tldr: This exploratory mixed-methods study examines residents’ values, concerns, and expectations before developing an AI smartphone tool that estimates parcel-level wildfire risk from property photographs. Among 30 Los Angeles County residents, receptivity was cautious but generally positive: 66.7% indicated likely or very likely use. Privacy and data security were the leading concerns, while cost was the primary barrier to implementing recommendations. The study proposes an AI Value Map with nine dimensions to convert early community input into traceable design requirements for resident-facing hazard tools.
AI.motivation: The study addresses a common limitation in resident-facing AI hazard communication: community feedback is often collected only after key decisions about data governance, privacy, explainability, and system functionality have already been made. The authors therefore seek to understand residents’ values, concerns, and practical expectations before building the predictive model or interface, with the goal of grounding system design in community priorities and anticipating negative consequences.
AI.method: The researchers used a convergent mixed-methods design. They surveyed 30 Los Angeles County residents, and seven of these participants also joined a virtual town hall. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and exploratory false-discovery-rate-adjusted Spearman correlations. Qualitative open-ended and town hall responses were analyzed through inductive thematic coding. Findings were synthesized into an AI Value Map containing nine value dimensions, provisional design requirements, and potential consequences of failing to address those requirements.
AI.result: Participants were cautiously receptive: 66.7% reported being likely or very likely to use the proposed tool. They associated fair risk assessment with the inclusion of relevant property and neighborhood conditions. Privacy and data security were the most frequently reported concerns (64.3%), and cost was the main obstacle to acting on mitigation recommendations (65.5%). Tool-use likelihood was strongly associated with willingness to save or share risk results (ρ = 0.752, pFDR < .001). The qualitative and quantitative findings were translated into nine community-grounded value dimensions and corresponding design implications.
AI.conclusion: The study provides preliminary evidence that residents may accept AI-based wildfire risk tools when issues of fairness, contextual relevance, privacy, security, interpretability, uncertainty, and affordability are addressed. Its main contribution is procedural: the AI Value Map offers a pre-model method for converting early community input into explicit, traceable design constraints. Because the sample was small and geographically limited, the findings should be treated as exploratory rather than broadly generalizable.

title: Sycophancy Through a Five-Level AI Response Validation Framework
summary: AI sycophancy, the tendency of AI systems to excessively agree with, flatter, or validate users, is an emerging concern in human-AI interaction. It is especially consequential in problem-sharing contexts, where users may seek both information and emotional validation. This paper conceptualizes AI sycophancy as excessive response validation and introduces a five-level AI Response Validation Framework (ARVF), measured using a six-item Perceived AI Sycophancy Scale (PASS). Across three phases, the study validated the framework with human participants through an online questionnaire, tested LLM-as-evaluators in answering PASS, and examined how ten contemporary LLMs generated and evaluated responses to real-world work and personal conflict scenarios. Results supported the intended progression of perceived sycophancy in ARVF and the reliability of PASS. Trust and perceived competence followed an inverted U-shaped pattern. LLM ratings reproduced the five-level structure but showed calibration differences from human ratings. Based on the LLM ratings, the ten contemporary LLMs were grouped according to their behavioral pattern. Text-based analysis provided further support on the linguistical structure for sycophantic responses generated by LLMs. Findings highlight AI sycophancy as a graded, context-sensitive interactional phenomenon.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and validates a five-level framework for measuring AI sycophancy—excessive agreement, flattery, or validation—in problem-sharing interactions. It introduces a six-item Perceived AI Sycophancy Scale (PASS), compares human and LLM evaluations, and analyzes ten contemporary LLMs across work and personal conflict scenarios. Results show that sycophancy is graded and context-sensitive; trust and perceived competence peak at moderate validation, while LLM evaluators reproduce the framework with calibration differences from humans.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the lack of a systematic, empirically validated way to define and measure AI sycophancy, particularly when users share problems and expect both useful information and emotional support. Excessive validation may undermine accuracy and decision quality, while insufficient validation may reduce trust and perceived support. The study therefore seeks to clarify how different degrees of response validation affect user perceptions and how consistently humans and LLMs identify sycophantic behavior.
AI.method: The study uses three phases: (1) human participants evaluate responses representing five levels of validation using an online questionnaire, supporting the AI Response Validation Framework (ARVF) and validating the six-item Perceived AI Sycophancy Scale (PASS); (2) LLM-as-evaluators assess responses using PASS, allowing comparison with human judgments; and (3) ten contemporary LLMs generate and evaluate responses to real-world work and personal conflict scenarios. The authors also apply text-based linguistic analysis to identify structural features associated with sycophantic responses and group models by behavioral patterns.
AI.result: Human evaluations supported the intended five-level progression of perceived sycophancy and indicated that PASS is reliable. Trust and perceived competence exhibited an inverted U-shaped relationship with validation, suggesting that moderate validation is viewed more favorably than either minimal or excessive validation. LLM evaluators recovered the five-level structure but differed from humans in rating calibration. The ten evaluated LLMs formed distinct behavioral groups, and linguistic analysis identified textual patterns associated with sycophantic responses.
AI.conclusion: AI sycophancy is not a binary property but a graded, context-sensitive interactional phenomenon. Moderate response validation may optimize trust and perceived competence, whereas excessive validation can become sycophantic. ARVF and PASS provide initial tools for studying and benchmarking this behavior, although differences between human and LLM judgments indicate that evaluator calibration remains important.

title: Designing Adaptive Affective Chatbots for Online Learning: Trade-offs Between User Control, Automation, and Transparency
summary:
Online students often face emotional challenges such as frustration, isolation, and fluctuating motivation, which can hinder sustained engagement in online learning. While affective chatbots have shown promise in healthcare and wellness, most learning support chatbots focus primarily on cognitive assistance with limited attention to learners' emotional and motivational experiences. In this work, we investigate how adaptive affective chatbot support can be designed for online learning through an iterative design process.
  Through a mixed-methods needfinding study (n=38), we identified substantial variation in how learners respond to affective support, with no single strategy universally preferred. This led us to develop three adaptive design alternatives: user-controlled, AI-driven, and hybrid co-controlled adaptation, and examine key trade-offs between automation, transparency, and user control. A final evaluation (n=25) showed that 88% of participants favored the adaptive hybrid design over a non-adaptive alternative, highlighting the value of balancing transparency, user control, and interaction simplicity. We discuss design implications for adaptive affective chatbot systems in emotionally challenging online learning contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates adaptive affective chatbots for emotionally challenging online learning. Through iterative mixed-methods design, it identifies diverse learner preferences, develops user-controlled, AI-driven, and hybrid adaptation strategies, and finds that most participants prefer the hybrid approach to a non-adaptive chatbot.
AI.motivation: Online learners frequently experience frustration, isolation, and changing motivation, yet existing educational chatbots mainly provide cognitive assistance and offer limited emotional or motivational support. Because learners differ substantially in how they prefer to receive affective support, the study addresses the need for adaptive chatbot designs that balance personalization with transparency and user control.
AI.method: The researchers used an iterative design process. First, a mixed-methods needfinding study with 38 participants examined learners’ responses to affective support. Based on the observed variation in preferences, they developed and compared three adaptation approaches: user-controlled, AI-driven, and hybrid co-controlled adaptation. A final evaluation with 25 participants compared the adaptive designs, particularly the hybrid design, with a non-adaptive alternative, focusing on trade-offs involving automation, transparency, user control, and interaction simplicity.
AI.result: The needfinding study found no universally preferred affective-support strategy, indicating substantial variation among learners. In the final evaluation, 88% of participants preferred the adaptive hybrid design over the non-adaptive alternative. The findings suggest that combining AI adaptation with user oversight can better satisfy learners’ needs while preserving transparency and control.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive affective chatbots for online learning should accommodate individual differences rather than apply a single support strategy. A hybrid co-controlled design appears especially promising because it balances personalization and automation with transparency, user control, and simple interaction. The paper provides design implications for emotionally supportive chatbot systems in online education.

title: viaCross: A Pen-Based Technique for Selecting Objects and Attributes of Interest using Crossing-Based Gestures
summary: Crossing-based selection is well-studied, yet past research has overlooked multi-object and attribute selection with crossing gestures. We present viaCross, a pen-based technique in which crossing strokes define attribute constraints, paired with attribute widgets that visualize and allow subsequent edits to these constraints. A controlled study compared viaCross with traditional WIMP filter panels. Results show that viaCross was more efficient for complex object-level selections, requiring fewer strokes and maintaining efficiency as task difficulty increased. WIMP panels were faster and more intuitive for simple attribute-based selections, but participants encountered repeated deselections and occasional misclicks. viaCross matched panel performance for creating attribute selections but was slower during refinement, as widgets had to be recreated, indicating the need for persistent widgets or hybrid support with a WIMP-style interface. Overall, viaCross demonstrates that crossing-based gestures can provide an efficient and scalable approach to multi-object and attribute selection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces viaCross, a pen-based crossing-gesture technique for selecting multiple objects and specifying attribute constraints. In a controlled comparison with WIMP filter panels, viaCross was more efficient for complex object selections, while WIMP was faster and more intuitive for simple attribute filtering. The findings support crossing-based selection as scalable, but suggest persistent widgets or hybrid interfaces for efficient refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing crossing-based selection research has primarily focused on simpler selection scenarios and has not adequately addressed multi-object selection combined with attribute-based constraints. The paper aims to determine whether crossing gestures can efficiently support these more complex tasks and how they compare with conventional WIMP filter panels.
AI.method: The authors developed viaCross, a pen-based technique in which crossing strokes specify attribute constraints and attribute widgets visualize and enable later editing of those constraints. They conducted a controlled user study comparing viaCross with traditional WIMP-based filter panels across object-level selection, attribute selection, and refinement tasks of varying difficulty. Performance and interaction issues such as stroke count, speed, intuitiveness, deselection, and misclicks were examined.
AI.result: viaCross required fewer strokes and remained efficient as object-selection difficulty increased, outperforming WIMP panels for complex object-level selections. WIMP panels were faster and more intuitive for simple attribute-based selections, although they produced repeated deselections and occasional misclicks. viaCross was comparable to WIMP for initially creating attribute selections but slower for refinement because widgets had to be recreated.
AI.conclusion: Crossing-based gestures can offer an efficient and scalable solution for multi-object and attribute selection. However, refinement should be improved through persistent attribute widgets or a hybrid design that combines viaCross with WIMP-style controls.

title: Assessing Acceptance and Privacy Preferences of Third-party Financial Data Sharing in Bipolar Disorder
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, preregistration available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/5AKEB
summary: Bipolar disorder is strongly associated with financial instability. We examine how different interventions motivate individuals with bipolar disorder to share financial data with others. This approach can inform the development of tools for digital monitoring and intervention designed to promote financial stability in this population. 500 individuals with BD completed a pre-registered factorial vignette survey to examine level of comfort with hypothetical scenarios involving third-party financial interventions during symptomatic and euthymic periods. Scenario components were systematically varied between third-party actors, mood states, and intervention types. Participants rated sharing comfort on a 0-10 point scale. Multilevel models tested differences alongside clinical and financial histories, relational trust, and personality. Participants were most comfortable involving care partners in financial planning. They were more comfortable with temporary spending restrictions during symptomatic states than euthymic periods, underscoring the importance of accurate mood detection for intervention delivery. Prior financial help-seeking behavior and higher relational trust predicted greater comfort. Bankruptcy experience --- declared by 11.4% and considered by 31.7% --- was associated with increased comfort with spending restrictions. Individuals with psychiatric advance directives (8%) were significantly more comfortable sharing spending behaviors than those without. Comfort with financial interventions was higher among those with prior financial challenges or help-seeking histories. Participants distinguished between symptomatic and euthymic periods, favoring targeted, time-limited restrictions over general monitoring. These findings extend prior work on financial data sharing for illness self-management.

AI.tldr: A preregistered factorial vignette study of 500 people with bipolar disorder found that comfort with sharing financial data and accepting interventions depended on the trusted third party, mood state, and intervention type. Participants generally preferred care-partner involvement and targeted, temporary spending restrictions during symptomatic periods. Prior financial difficulties, help-seeking, relational trust, and psychiatric advance directives were associated with greater comfort.
AI.motivation: Bipolar disorder is associated with financial instability, yet the acceptability of third-party financial monitoring and interventions is not well understood. The study aims to identify which actors and intervention designs people with bipolar disorder find acceptable, supporting the development of person-centered digital tools for financial self-management and stability.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a preregistered factorial vignette survey with 500 individuals with bipolar disorder. Hypothetical scenarios systematically varied the third-party actor, mood state (symptomatic versus euthymic), and intervention type. Participants rated their comfort with sharing financial information on a 0–10 scale. Multilevel models examined differences while accounting for clinical and financial histories, relational trust, and personality factors.
AI.result: Participants were most comfortable involving care partners in financial planning. They preferred temporary spending restrictions during symptomatic periods over restrictions during euthymic periods, indicating that intervention timing and accurate mood detection are important. Greater comfort was associated with prior financial help-seeking, higher relational trust, previous financial challenges, bankruptcy experience, and having a psychiatric advance directive. Participants favored targeted, time-limited restrictions over broad or continuous monitoring.
AI.conclusion: Acceptable financial interventions for bipolar disorder should be collaborative, trust-based, and sensitive to mood state. Care-partner involvement and narrowly targeted, temporary restrictions may be more acceptable than general monitoring, particularly when preferences are established in advance. The findings support personalized digital interventions but also highlight the need for reliable mood detection, user autonomy, and further evaluation beyond hypothetical scenarios.

title: A study on human-agent teaming through spoken interaction: the impact of human individual traits and agent characteristics
summary: Human-agent teams are collaborative systems where humans and agents work interdependently to achieve shared goals. The success of such teams is associated with the human's perception of the agent as a legitimate teammate. This perception is thought to depend not only on the agent's capabilities and reliability but also on social factors. We explore whether simple changes in an agent's communicative behavior can influence the human's perception of the agent's teammate-likeness. To this end, we developed a protocol based on a collaborative game requiring spoken interaction, in which a human subject and a virtual agent collaborate to identify a target object and place it on a board. Each subject interacted with two agents which provided the same task-relevant information but differed in behavior. While one was a neutral tool-like agent, the other was a team-building agent that used simple social strategies such as empathy, politeness, and positivity. Our analysis shows that the team-building agent was perceived as significantly more teammate-like, even in terms of its ability, despite both agents having identical capabilities for game-solving. Further, subjects with a higher propensity to trust automated systems and lower neuroticism tended to have a more favorable perception of the agent. Finally, we found that subjects tended to change their prosodic patterns when talking to the team-building agent, as a classifier based on prosodic features was able to predict the type of agent with better-than-random performance. A practically relevant conclusion is that minimal changes in spoken communication behavior of the agent, easily implemented in a variety of scenarios, can have a significant positive impact on the human's perception of its teammate-likeness.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that simple social behaviors in an agent’s spoken communication—such as empathy, politeness, and positivity—substantially increase how teammate-like and capable the agent is perceived, even when objective task capabilities are identical. Human trust propensity and neuroticism also shape these evaluations, and participants’ speech prosody changes in response to the agent’s social style.
AI.motivation: Human-agent team effectiveness depends partly on whether people perceive an agent as a legitimate teammate rather than merely a tool. Existing work emphasizes capability and reliability, but the abstract argues that social communication may also influence teammate perception. The study therefore examines whether minimal, easily deployable changes in an agent’s spoken behavior can improve perceived teammate-likeness.
AI.method: The researchers created a spoken collaborative-game protocol in which a human and a virtual agent jointly identified a target object and placed it on a board. Each participant interacted with two agents that delivered identical task-relevant information and had identical game-solving capabilities: a neutral, tool-like agent and a team-building agent using empathy, politeness, and positivity. They compared participants’ perceptions of the agents, examined relationships with individual differences in trust propensity and neuroticism, and used prosodic-feature classification to test whether participants’ speech changed depending on the agent type.
AI.result: The team-building agent was rated significantly more teammate-like than the neutral agent, including in perceived ability, despite equivalent objective capabilities. Participants who generally trusted automated systems more and reported lower neuroticism tended to evaluate the agent more favorably. A classifier using participants’ prosodic features predicted which agent they were speaking with above chance, indicating that the agent’s social style affected human vocal behavior.
AI.conclusion: Small changes in spoken social behavior can positively influence human perceptions of an agent’s teammate-likeness without changing its functional capabilities. Designing agents with basic empathy, politeness, and positivity may therefore improve human-agent collaboration, while user traits and adaptive changes in human communication should also be considered.

title: LINK: A Corpus-Grounded Design Pattern Library for Educational Technologies
summary: Designing learning interfaces is often an ill-structured problem: effective solutions depend on learning goals, subject matter, learner characteristics, and interaction context that are difficult to generalize. Designers must integrate knowledge from learning sciences, interaction design, and subject domains when translating learning goals into interface decisions. Yet, prior efforts to connect learning theory and design have largely focused on learning activities or specific technologies, leaving interface-level design knowledge fragmented across systems. In this work, we take a bottom-up approach to surface this knowledge from existing educational interfaces. We present LINK (Linking INstructional Knowledge to interfaces), a library of 27 recurring interface patterns, organized under nine higher-level design commitments, which describe broader learning-science-grounded goals for interfaces. As part of developing LINK, we conducted a user study (N=14) with designers to evaluate LINK's generative power. Our findings suggest that LINK helps designers generate interface ideas and articulate theory-grounded rationales for design decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LINK, a library of 27 recurring educational interface patterns organized around nine learning-science-grounded design commitments. A study with 14 designers indicates that LINK supports idea generation and helps designers explain interface decisions using theory-based rationales.
AI.motivation: Educational interface design is ill-structured and context-dependent, requiring designers to integrate learning science, interaction design, and domain knowledge. Existing approaches often focus on activities or technologies rather than interface-level knowledge, leaving reusable design guidance fragmented.
AI.method: The authors take a bottom-up approach by examining existing educational interfaces and synthesizing recurring design knowledge into LINK. LINK contains 27 interface patterns grouped under nine broader design commitments. They evaluate its generative usefulness through a user study with 14 designers, assessing whether the library helps participants develop interface concepts and articulate learning-theory-grounded rationales.
AI.result: The study suggests that LINK helps designers generate new interface ideas and provide theory-grounded explanations for their design choices. The abstract does not report quantitative results, comparison conditions, or detailed participant outcomes.
AI.conclusion: LINK offers a structured, reusable vocabulary for connecting learning-science principles with educational interface decisions. It appears useful as a generative design resource, although broader validation is needed across designers, domains, and real-world design settings.

title: DimSteer: Steering LLM Authoring with Automatically Discovered Stylistic Controls
summary: Large language model writing interfaces often make users steer outputs by repeatedly articulating desired changes in natural language. Yet writers may recognize useful stylistic directions only after seeing alternatives, making revision recall-heavy. We present DimSteer, an authoring interface that samples prompt-local completions, discovers high-variance activation-space axes of variation, labels them, and exposes them as sliders with pole previews, diff comparison, and reset controls. Users can manipulate discovered dimensions, reducing the need to reformulate prompts for each stylistic adjustment. In a within-subjects study with 16 participants against a matched prompt-only baseline, DimSteer reduced mental demand, effort, and frustration while preserving comparable perceived success. Participants valued the surfaced dimensions, yet 15 of 16 disagreed that they would have thought to request the same changes in a prompt. Results suggest prompt-local controls can shift LLM authoring from recall-based prompting toward recognition-based exploration and direct manipulation, while preserving prompting for open-ended edits.

AI.tldr: DimSteer is an LLM writing interface that automatically discovers prompt-local stylistic variation directions and exposes them as interactive controls. In a 16-person within-subjects study, it reduced perceived mental demand, effort, and frustration relative to prompt-only interaction without reducing perceived success.
AI.motivation: Conventional LLM writing interfaces require users to repeatedly describe desired revisions in natural language. This is recall-heavy because users may not know which stylistic changes are useful until they see alternatives. The paper addresses the need for an interface that supports recognition-based exploration and direct manipulation while retaining prompting for open-ended requests.
AI.method: DimSteer samples completions for a given prompt, identifies high-variance axes in activation space, labels the discovered dimensions, and presents them as sliders. The interface includes previews at slider poles, side-by-side diff comparison, and reset controls. It was evaluated in a within-subjects study with 16 participants against a matched prompt-only baseline, measuring workload-related experiences and perceived task success.
AI.result: Compared with the prompt-only baseline, DimSteer reduced mental demand, effort, and frustration while maintaining comparable perceived success. Participants valued the surfaced stylistic dimensions, and 15 of 16 participants reported that they would not have thought to request the same changes through prompts.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-local latent-space controls can shift LLM authoring from recall-based prompting toward recognition-based exploration and direct manipulation. DimSteer complements rather than replaces prompting: sliders support discovered stylistic adjustments, while natural-language prompts remain useful for open-ended edits. The findings are promising but should be interpreted in light of the small sample and controlled within-subjects evaluation.

title: Evaluating Just Noticeable Differences in Layered Opacity Visualizations
summary: Opacity is a widely used channel in data visualization, but it remains less well understood compared to channels such as color, length, size, etc. Recent work from Meng et al. investigated the impact of opacity across competing color schemes, finding that certain color schemes were associated with better participant accuracy. We examine these effects further in a controlled two-alternative forced-choice setup to determine whether opacity differences are truly equal across possible opacity comparison ranges. In a within-subjects study with 96 trials, including two competing color schemes (best and worst from Meng et al.) and 48 opacity pairs, we find little differences between color schemes but larger individual differences in accuracy. Further, results show stable performance in middle opacity ranges, with more errors occurring when comparing extreme values. We discuss potential implications for design guidelines and further study and make our study materials, analysis scripts, and data available at https://osf.io/zv9dx/overview?view_only=38d03cea1b3d42788593e3e6b1016cfd.

AI.tldr: A controlled within-subjects study tests how accurately people compare opacity differences across two color schemes and 48 opacity pairs. Color scheme had little effect, while individual differences were larger; comparisons were more reliable for middle opacities and less accurate at extreme values.
AI.motivation: Opacity is common in visualization but less well understood than channels such as color, length, and size. Prior work reported that color scheme influenced opacity-comparison accuracy, so this study investigates whether that effect is robust and whether opacity differences are equally discriminable across the full opacity range.
AI.method: The authors conducted a within-subjects two-alternative forced-choice experiment. Participants completed 96 trials involving two competing color schemes selected from prior work—one previously associated with the best performance and one with the worst—and 48 pairs of opacity values. Accuracy was analyzed across color schemes, opacity ranges, and participants. Study materials, scripts, and data were openly shared.
AI.result: Performance differed little between the two color schemes, contrary to the stronger color-scheme effect suggested by the earlier study. Individual differences in accuracy were comparatively larger. Accuracy was relatively stable for middle opacity ranges but decreased when participants compared extreme opacity values.
AI.conclusion: Opacity comparisons are not equally reliable across the entire opacity scale. Visualization guidance should account for reduced discriminability at extreme values and substantial user-to-user variation, rather than relying heavily on color scheme alone. Further replication and investigation are warranted.

title: Benchmarking Psychological Dynamics in Generative Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to simulate human behavior, acting as computational replicas of human subjects. Yet the lived psychological experience of humans is difficult to benchmark, particularly as it unfolds over time. We introduce a psychometric benchmark for computational replicas: personas that carry a fixed identity through an evolving sequence of events. Built entirely from published norms and meta-analytic effects, the benchmark scores two dimensions of psychological realism. The first, internal validity, quantifies whether generated trajectories reproduce the internal structure of repeated human measurement: distributions, the between- versus within-person variance partition, temporal dependence, and range. The second, external validity, quantifies whether replicas recover established trait, state, and indicator relations. Across 36 open-weight and proprietary LLMs from nine developers (1B-671B parameters), most recover the direction of established relations (84.3% mean agreement) and the variance partition (26 of 34), yet the within-person correlation and distributional structure elude recovery. Internal validity is independent of scale and capability: a mid-size open LLM (Gemma-3-27B) strikes the best trade-off between the two dimensions. The benchmark is a precondition for using computational replicas in causal inference across domains (e.g., marketing, healthcare), and identifies within-person grounding as the central challenge ahead.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a psychometric benchmark for evaluating whether LLM-based personas realistically reproduce human psychological behavior over time. Across 36 models, LLMs generally recover known relation directions and variance partitioning, but fail to reproduce within-person correlations and distributional structure. Psychological realism appears largely independent of model size, with Gemma-3-27B offering the strongest trade-off.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as computational replicas of people, but existing evaluations do not adequately test whether these replicas reproduce lived psychological dynamics across repeated events. The paper addresses the lack of a principled, longitudinal benchmark for measuring psychological realism and for determining whether such replicas are reliable enough for applications such as causal inference.
AI.method: The authors construct a psychometric benchmark entirely from published normative data and meta-analytic effects. Personas retain a fixed identity while responding to evolving sequences of events. Performance is evaluated along two dimensions: internal validity, measuring distributions, between-person versus within-person variance, temporal dependence, and range; and external validity, measuring recovery of established relations among traits, states, and indicators. The benchmark is applied to 36 open-weight and proprietary LLMs from nine developers, ranging from 1B to 671B parameters.
AI.result: Models show relatively strong external validity, with 84.3% mean agreement on the direction of established relations, and reproduce the variance partition in 26 of 34 evaluated cases. However, they generally fail to recover within-person correlations and distributional structure. Internal validity is not reliably associated with model scale or general capability. Gemma-3-27B provides the best balance between internal and external validity among the evaluated systems.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark establishes a necessary foundation for evaluating LLM-based computational replicas. Current models can reproduce some population-level psychological relations but lack faithful within-person grounding and realistic distributional dynamics. Improving longitudinal, person-specific behavior should therefore be the central research priority before using computational replicas for causal inference or other high-stakes behavioral applications.

title: Neurodiversity-Aware Multimodal Affective Computing for Neurodevelopmental Assessment: From Norm-Referenced Classification to Context-Sensitive Decision Support
summary: Automated neurodevelopmental assessment increasingly combines computer vision, speech, eye tracking, physiology, and machine learning, yet multimodality and discrimination do not establish construct validity, clinical usefulness, or appropriate interpretation of behavioral variation. We propose a testable architecture for neurodiversity-aware multimodal affective computing in which population-relative deviation is not treated as sufficient evidence of adverse functioning. This conceptual article reports neither a new participant-level study nor a trained predictive system, and no predictive or clinical superiority is claimed. The framework keeps observable signals, modality quality and availability, context, population-relative information, pooled within-person references and, when sufficiently supported, context-conditioned within person references, and predictive uncertainty distinguishable throughout inference. It defines structured decision-support outputs and auditable requirements for target validity, temporal integrity, contextual leakage, missing-modality robustness, calibration, subgroup evaluation, interpretability, privacy, and human decision boundaries. The contribution is architectural rather than algorithmic: it specifies empirically testable constraints that can be instantiated with different multimodal learning methods. Autism provides the principal motivating evidence base, without assuming unchanged transfer to other neurodevelopmental conditions.

AI.tldr: A conceptual, neurodiversity-aware architecture for multimodal affective computing that separates behavioral observation from interpretation and requires empirical validation before clinical or functional claims.
AI.motivation: Existing automated neurodevelopmental assessment systems often conflate multimodal prediction or population-relative behavioral deviation with construct validity, adverse functioning, and clinical usefulness. The paper addresses this interpretive and validation gap, especially for autism-related assessment, while recognizing behavioral variation without pathologizing difference.
AI.method: The authors propose a conceptual architecture rather than a new dataset, participant-level experiment, or trained predictive model. The framework maintains separate representations for observable signals, modality quality and availability, context, population-relative information, pooled within-person references, context-conditioned within-person references when justified, and predictive uncertainty. It also specifies structured decision-support outputs and auditable requirements concerning target validity, temporal integrity, contextual leakage, missing-modality robustness, calibration, subgroup evaluation, interpretability, privacy, and human decision boundaries.
AI.result: No empirical performance results are reported, and no predictive or clinical superiority is claimed. The primary outcome is a set of testable architectural constraints that can be implemented using different multimodal learning approaches and evaluated in future studies.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal neurodevelopmental assessment should not infer adverse functioning from deviation alone. Reliable and ethically interpretable systems require explicit separation of measurement and interpretation, context-sensitive and appropriately supported within-person references, uncertainty reporting, robustness to missing data, subgroup evaluation, privacy safeguards, and clearly defined human oversight. Autism is the main motivating evidence base, so transfer to other neurodevelopmental conditions remains unestablished.

title: VoCa: Designing Speech-Canvas Interaction for Voice-Based Conversational Agents
summary: People write and sketch while speaking to explain, organize, and develop content together. Inspired by these practices, we investigate how voice agents can use a canvas alongside speech in multi-turn conversations with users. We conducted a two-part formative study: an observational study of how pairs coordinated speech and boardwork, followed by a design workshop that informed a design space for speech-canvas interaction with voice agents. Building on these insights, we developed VoCa, a voice agent that coordinates speech with visual object creation, annotation, and attention guidance. A five-day deployment with 18 participants examined usability, experiences of speech-canvas interaction, patterns of use, and desired improvements. Participants' experiences highlighted opportunities for speech-canvas interaction in learning, work, and daily life, alongside challenges in coordinating what agents say and show in ways users can follow and influence. These findings inform how voice agents can use a canvas alongside speech in conversation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how voice agents can combine spoken dialogue with a shared visual canvas. It presents formative studies, introduces the VoCa prototype, and evaluates it in a five-day deployment with 18 participants. The findings identify promising applications and coordination challenges in speech-canvas interaction.
AI.motivation: Voice-only interaction can be limited when users need to organize, externalize, or jointly develop information. Since people naturally combine speech with writing and sketching, the paper explores whether voice agents can similarly coordinate spoken communication with visual content on a canvas.
AI.method: The research used a two-part formative study: an observational study of pairs coordinating speech and boardwork, followed by a design workshop. These results informed a design space for speech-canvas interaction. The authors then developed VoCa, a voice agent capable of creating visual objects, annotating them, and guiding user attention. A five-day field deployment with 18 participants assessed usability, user experiences, usage patterns, and desired improvements.
AI.result: Participants found potential value for speech-canvas interaction across learning, work, and everyday activities. The deployment also revealed difficulties in coordinating the agent’s verbal explanations and visual actions, particularly when users needed to track, understand, or influence both modalities. The study generated insights into usage patterns and design improvements for multimodal voice agents.
AI.conclusion: Voice agents can benefit from using a canvas as a conversational visual companion, but effective interaction requires careful synchronization between speech and visual output, as well as mechanisms that let users guide and influence what appears. The paper provides design implications for developing multimodal agents that support collaborative explanation, organization, and content creation.

title: Trends in EHR Satisfaction and Interoperability Among Family Physicians: A Five-Year Analysis of the ABFM Continuous Certification Questionnaire, 2022-2026
comment: 32 Pages, 4 Tables, 6 Figures, 8 Supplement Tables, 6 Supplement Figures
summary:
Objective: To assess trends in family physicians' (FPs) electronic health record (EHR) satisfaction and their experience of interoperability across organizations.
  Materials and Methods: Serial cross-sectional analysis of five waves of the American Board of Family Medicine's Continuous Certification Questionnaire (2022-26). Adjusted logistic regression compared odds of being very satisfied across 11 EHRs; Cochran-Armitage tests assessed vendor trends. Ease of using outside information was analyzed separately for same- and different-vendor sources.
  Results: Across 36,785 FPs, adjusted odds of being very satisfied relative to Epic ranged from 0.91 (95% CI, 0.74-1.11) for Elation Health to 0.17 (95% CI, 0.15-0.20) for Oracle Health/Cerner. Only Epic's users became significantly more satisfied (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P < .001), widening the vendor satisfaction gap. Within comparable periods, ease of using different-vendor information did not improve; fewer than 13% rated it very easy. Epic's interoperability advantage reversed by exchange type: non-Epic users had less than half the odds of Epic users of rating same-vendor interoperability very easy (adjusted OR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.38-0.44) but 1.54 times the odds for different-vendor interoperability (95% CI, 1.35-1.75).
  Discussion and Conclusion: The ABFM data are already informing EHR policy effects but they also have utility for the EHR marketplace. EHR satisfaction differences are widening, and reported ease of using different-vendor information is low and unchanged. While EHR satisfaction has known implications for burden and burnout, interoperability is a quality and safety threat that may be compounded by artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: This serial cross-sectional study of 36,785 family physicians found widening differences in satisfaction across EHR vendors, with Epic showing the only significant improvement and Oracle Health/Cerner substantially lower satisfaction. Interoperability across different vendors remained difficult, with fewer than 13% rating it very easy.
AI.motivation: The study addresses persistent concerns that EHR usability, vendor differences, and poor interoperability contribute to clinician burden, burnout, and risks to care quality and safety. It also examines whether interoperability performance differs depending on whether information comes from the same or a different EHR vendor.
AI.method: Researchers analyzed five waves of the American Board of Family Medicine Continuous Certification Questionnaire from 2022–2026. They used adjusted logistic regression to compare the odds of being very satisfied across 11 EHR vendors, Cochran–Armitage tests to assess trends over time, and separate analyses of the ease of accessing information from same-vendor versus different-vendor systems.
AI.result: Among 36,785 family physicians, adjusted satisfaction relative to Epic varied substantially, from an odds ratio of 0.91 for Elation Health to 0.17 for Oracle Health/Cerner. Only Epic users showed a significant increase in satisfaction, leading to a widening satisfaction gap. Fewer than 13% of physicians rated access to different-vendor information as very easy. Compared with Epic users, non-Epic users had lower odds of finding same-vendor interoperability very easy (OR 0.41) but higher odds for different-vendor interoperability (OR 1.54), indicating that Epic’s advantage was specific to same-vendor exchange.
AI.conclusion: EHR satisfaction disparities are increasing, while cross-vendor interoperability remains poor and shows no meaningful improvement. These findings are relevant to EHR policy and market evaluation and suggest that inadequate interoperability may create quality and safety risks, potentially intensified by the integration of artificial intelligence into clinical workflows.

title: Proactive AI: From Turns to Replannable Dialogue Timelines
summary: Conventional large-language-model chat interfaces typically follow user-initiated turns: each request elicits a response, after which the system waits for further input. Human asynchronous communication instead unfolds over time through message bursts, delays, silence, resumed topics, and self-initiated contact. Proactive dialogue therefore requires not only deciding when to speak, but also managing pending conversational actions and allowing them to be revised as context evolves. We introduce Proactive AI, a framework for proactive dialogue built around replannable temporal message queues. The framework treats interaction as a continuous event timeline and unsent conversational actions as revisable state. A user event, dialogue-pacemaker event, or scheduled decision may yield silence, one or more immediate messages, or future conversational actions. The system may also observe a user message without an immediate visible response and defer the response decision. Before delivery, every planned message must be reconsidered against the current context; reaching a scheduled time does not itself authorize delivery. We provide a formal semantics that characterizes when future conversational actions may be revised, withdrawn, or executed as context evolves. The framework extends AI participation beyond responses to current requests, enabling self-initiated exchanges without new requests, sustained follow-up over time, and revisions of subsequent actions as context evolves. It provides an executable basis for long-term human-AI interaction in tutoring, scientific collaboration, and everyday companionship.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Proactive AI, a formal and executable framework for asynchronous proactive dialogue using replannable temporal message queues. It models conversation as a continuous event timeline in which planned messages remain revisable until delivery, enabling silence, delayed responses, self-initiated contact, follow-up, and context-sensitive withdrawal or revision.
AI.motivation: Conventional chat systems are reactive and turn-based: they respond to explicit user requests and then wait. This poorly represents asynchronous human communication, which includes delays, message bursts, silence, resumed topics, and system-initiated contact. The paper addresses the need for AI systems to decide not only what to say, but also when to speak and how to revise pending actions as new context appears.
AI.method: The authors propose Proactive AI, centered on replannable temporal message queues. Interaction is represented as a continuous event timeline, while unsent conversational actions are treated as revisable state. User events, dialogue-pacemaker events, and scheduled decisions can produce no message, immediate messages, or future actions. The framework permits observing a user message without responding immediately, and requires every planned message to be reconsidered against current context before delivery. A formal semantics specifies when future actions can be revised, withdrawn, or executed.
AI.result: The framework supports proactive behaviors beyond direct request-response interaction, including self-initiated exchanges, delayed and sustained follow-up, silence, deferred responses, and context-dependent revision or cancellation of planned messages. It provides an executable basis for implementing these behaviors in long-term human-AI interaction.
AI.conclusion: Proactive dialogue should be modeled as temporal, stateful, and revisable rather than as a sequence of isolated request-response turns. By formalizing pending conversational actions and requiring pre-delivery reconsideration, Proactive AI offers a foundation for more flexible long-term interaction in tutoring, scientific collaboration, and companionship.

title: Preference vs. Performance: EEG-Based Classification of Learner Engagement in Multimodal Instruction
comment: Presented at The 26th IEEE International Conference on Advanced Learning Technologies (ICALT) 2026, July 6-9, 2026 at Hung Yen, Vietnam
summary: Effective adaptive instructional systems require robust measures of learner engagement that go beyond static user profiles. This study employs Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) to investigate the relationship between self-reported instructional modality preferences and objective neurophysiological markers of engagement. Thirty-seven participants engaged with learning content delivered via varying modalities (visual, auditory, reading/writing, kinesthetic). We captured real-time neural activity using two EEG devices: the Emotiv EpocX (14 channels, 128 Hz) and OpenBCI (16 channels, 125 Hz). Preferences were assessed using the VARK questionnaire. Consistent with literature challenging the "meshing hypothesis," aligning instructional modality with stated preferences did not significantly predict performance gains. However, spectral analysis of EEG data revealed divergent engagement patterns: when content aligned with preferences, distinct neural activity patterns emerged in theta and alpha frequency bands-markers associated with attention and cognitive processing. These signals were used to train a binary logistic regression classifier, achieving a mean accuracy of 83.21% with OpenBCI and 56.27% with Emotiv EpocX. These findings suggest that while self-reported preferences may not dictate learning outcomes, they significantly influence neurophysiological engagement, offering a viable, non-invasive input for adaptive educational algorithms.

AI.tldr: This study examines whether learners’ self-reported VARK preferences correspond to objective EEG indicators of engagement. Preference-aligned instruction did not significantly improve performance, but it produced distinguishable theta- and alpha-band EEG patterns. These patterns supported binary classification of engagement-related states, with substantially better accuracy for OpenBCI (83.21%) than Emotiv EpocX (56.27%).
AI.motivation: Static learner profiles and self-reported modality preferences may be insufficient for adaptive instructional systems. The study addresses whether multimodal learning analytics and real-time neurophysiological measurements can provide a more objective and dynamic indicator of learner engagement, while also testing the widely debated assumption that matching instruction to learner preferences improves learning outcomes.
AI.method: Thirty-seven participants studied content presented through visual, auditory, reading/writing, and kinesthetic modalities. Instructional preferences were measured using the VARK questionnaire. Neural activity was recorded during learning with two EEG systems: Emotiv EpocX, using 14 channels at 128 Hz, and OpenBCI, using 16 channels at 125 Hz. EEG spectral features, particularly in the theta and alpha bands associated with attention and cognitive processing, were analyzed. A binary logistic regression classifier was trained to distinguish engagement-related conditions or preference-aligned versus non-aligned states. Performance was evaluated using classification accuracy.
AI.result: Matching instructional modality to self-reported preference did not significantly predict improved learning performance, consistent with evidence against the meshing hypothesis. Nevertheless, preference-aligned conditions produced distinct theta- and alpha-band neural activity patterns. The classifier achieved a mean accuracy of 83.21% with OpenBCI and 56.27% with Emotiv EpocX, indicating device-dependent differences in signal quality or classification utility.
AI.conclusion: Self-reported modality preferences may not improve learning outcomes when used to match instructional delivery, but they appear to influence neurophysiological engagement patterns. EEG-derived signals, especially from OpenBCI in this study, may therefore provide a non-invasive input for adaptive educational systems. The findings support measuring engagement dynamically rather than relying exclusively on static learner profiles, while also highlighting the need to validate results across larger samples, devices, and learning contexts.

title: Rethinking Inline Citation Verification in Scholarly Communication
summary: Inline citations are central to scholarly communication, yet verifying their use is becoming increasingly challenging because of growing review pressures. We conducted a mixed-methods exploratory study to investigate how reviewers verify inline citations, the factors shaping their verification practices, and how they envision GenAI supporting this process. Across interviews (n=12) and a survey (n=203) of reviewers from HCI and AI venues, we found that reviewers' perceptions of citation importance, verification practices, and desired AI autonomy varied across citation types, reviewer characteristics, and research backgrounds. These findings highlight the need for adaptive support tailored to different citation types and reviewer practices, while revealing diverse preferences regarding the use of GenAI for this process. Moreover, effective citation verification should involve collaboration among reviewers, authors, and the broader research community, rather than relying solely on individual reviewers.

AI.tldr: This exploratory mixed-methods study examines how scholarly reviewers verify inline citations and how generative AI could support that task. Interviews with 12 reviewers and a survey of 203 HCI and AI reviewers show that citation importance, verification behavior, and preferred AI autonomy differ by citation type, reviewer characteristics, and research background. The paper argues for adaptive, collaborative citation-verification systems involving reviewers, authors, and the wider research community.
AI.motivation: The study is motivated by the increasing difficulty of verifying inline citations under growing peer-review pressures. Although citations are essential to scholarly communication, reviewers may lack sufficient time and consistent support to determine whether citations appropriately substantiate claims. The authors therefore investigate current verification practices and reviewer expectations for GenAI assistance.
AI.method: The authors use a mixed-methods exploratory design: semi-structured interviews with 12 reviewers and a survey of 203 reviewers from HCI and AI venues. The study examines how reviewers assess different citation types, which reviewer and background factors shape verification practices, and what levels of GenAI autonomy reviewers prefer.
AI.result: Reviewers differ in how important they consider various citation types, how they verify them, and how much autonomy they want GenAI to have. These differences are associated with citation type, reviewer characteristics, and research background. The findings indicate that a single uniform verification tool would be inadequate; support should adapt to both the citation and the reviewer. The study also identifies diverse expectations about GenAI involvement.
AI.conclusion: Citation verification should be supported through adaptive tools that reflect different citation types and reviewer practices, while accommodating varied preferences for GenAI autonomy. More broadly, reliable verification should be treated as a collaborative responsibility shared by reviewers, authors, and the research community, rather than as a task assigned solely to individual reviewers.

title: Optimizing AI-Driven Messaging for Type 2 Diabetes Management: Insights from Patient Preference Elicitation
comment: Forthcoming at the American Medical Informatics Association (AMIA) Annual Symposium, November 7-11, 2026
summary: Generative AI (GenAI) allows for improved user experience within conversational agents for diabetes management by supporting dynamic, context-aware conversations. In this study, we elicited patient preferences for the communication style of a GenAI-based conversational agent (uMatter) developed to support diabetes management. We conducted an online survey with 125 individuals with type 2 diabetes. The survey included a discrete choice experiment to evaluate participant preferences for different types of messaging attributes. The survey also elicited participant perceptions and feedback on the messages from uMatter. We found significant preference heterogeneity for the inclusion of emojis within the messages. Additionally, qualitative findings indicated that participants had different desired personas and communication styles for the conversational agent. We propose strategies from recent human-computer interaction and natural language processing research that can be used to design GenAI-based conversational agents that align with the communication preferences of patients.

AI.tldr: This study examines how people with type 2 diabetes prefer a generative-AI conversational agent to communicate. Using an online survey and discrete choice experiment with 125 participants, it found substantial variation in preferences, especially regarding emoji use, and identified differing desired personas and communication styles.
AI.motivation: Although generative AI can enable more personalized and context-aware diabetes-management support, its effectiveness depends on whether the agent communicates in ways patients find acceptable and engaging. The study therefore sought to identify patient preferences for message attributes, personas, and communication styles in the uMatter conversational agent.
AI.method: The researchers conducted an online survey of 125 individuals with type 2 diabetes. A discrete choice experiment assessed preferences for alternative messaging attributes, while additional survey questions collected participants’ perceptions and qualitative feedback on messages generated by uMatter.
AI.result: Participants showed significant preference heterogeneity regarding the inclusion of emojis, meaning that emoji use was not uniformly preferred. Qualitative responses also revealed diverse expectations for the agent’s persona and communication style. The study recommends applying human-computer interaction and natural language processing techniques to tailor conversational-agent communication to individual patient preferences.
AI.conclusion: GenAI conversational agents for diabetes management should avoid a one-size-fits-all communication style. Personalization of message features, emoji use, persona, and tone may improve acceptability and user experience. The findings provide design guidance, but further research should test whether preference alignment improves engagement and clinical outcomes.

title: Imagining a Muslim Internet: Trust, Autonomy, and Segregation in a Faith-Aligned Browser
